tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
In comments in one of my posts I came across a person with no risk target for his portfolio and a view that his job is to maximize return without regard to risk.  I said the job of every investor is to know what their risk tolerance is and hold a portfolio that takes roughly that risk.  Here's my comment

Here's what I do.  You decide if it's useful.  There is a level of change in my wealth that I find to be 1) absolute noise.  There is a level I find 2) slightly annoying.  A level I find that 3) pisses me off but doesn't upset me.  A level that that cause me to 4) loose sleep. A level that causes me to 5)  act to ease the pain.  Those are personal to me.  But I assure you everyone has levels like this.  I have learned that 4 and 5 are not something I am willing to experience.  I have and I don't want to again. So I operate somewhere in the range of 3-4.  Which for me place me at a risk target that I can manage and I acccept the expected return that it provides.  

IF you have never experienced all these levels it's fair to say you aren't taking enough risk but ideally you don't have to experience them and can just imagine them.   The risk of actually experiencing a level 5 event is it could turn into a level 6 event which could be a life changing loss or a level 7 which would be a loss so horrible you could not recover to anything like your current lifestyle. All of those risk levels are out there for you to experience and I encourage you to really understand that and hold a portfolio that takes risk but doesn't allow for 6-7 at all.  Even an unlevered portfolio is shockingly levered when you consider your future liabilities of paying for your lifestyle and your families education etc.

As someone that has had their data leaked once before in a breach from another hardware wallet, I am very wary of inputting my home address when ordering hardware devices.

And Trezor have also suffered from its delivery partners having their data leaked, so I think Trezor's new anonymous pickup is the perfect solution for both them as a company and all crypto users.

Across Europe, you can now order a Trezor under an alias, without sharing your home address, and have it shipped in a plain, unbranded box to a pickup location of your choosing. It’s still rolling out across different countries (if checkout doesn't show anonymous pickup, it isn't available in your country yet). The US is expected to follow soon.

Be also wary that when ordering online, paying by card means sharing some personal details with a third-party processor. If you pay in crypto they only receive the txn details.

Imo this should be the option anyone with any material sum of money in crypto uses going forward, and every hardware wallet should offer it by default. You should do your best to never connect your home address with crypto.

#Silver $ELEF.TO $SILEF

What does a Bolivian court ruling have to do with a 180 km truck haul?

That’s how far Silver Elephant has trucked silver-bearing rock from Apuradita to someone else’s mill in Potosí. The company wants to build its own mill at Apuradita, and the two other deposits it plans to feed into it are the ones at the heart of the ruling.

As @SilverElMining highlighted below, Bolivia’s Supreme Tribunal overturned the 2024 decision to cancel its subsidiary’s mining contract at Pulacayo and Paca. Paca alone supplied a third-party plant with more than 261,000 wet tonnes averaging 183 g/t silver in 2023–24.

That’s where I see the upside. All three deposits have already supplied outside mills. If Silver Elephant can permit and finance one mill to serve them all, shorter hauls and in-house processing could improve what it earns per tonne.

The next milestone I’m watching is the environmental assessment for the proposed 12,000-tonne-a-day plant. Management aims to file by year-end and expects a licence decision by June 2027.

#Uranium $MYRUF $M.CN

Of the 100 companies in my uranium cash table below, Myriad is one I’d watch for a rebound. It reported C$11.54M in cash and equivalents at July 31. Management says it can fund drilling beyond the first 5,000 metres of Phase II at Copper Mountain in Wyoming.

What I like is where those metres are going. Union Pacific drilled roughly 2,000 holes in this district decades ago. Myriad now owns Copper Mountain outright and can use that work to choose where a new hole will tell it the most. The aim is to verify historical results and fill the gaps needed for a first NI 43-101 mineral resource estimate.

The October 28 update gives a sense of what they’re finding. At Hesitation, one hole returned 34.3 metres at 399 ppm eU₃O₈ in preliminary downhole gamma readings. I’m watching the lab assays next.

Then there’s what Myriad picked up in Argentina. On November 2, it announced the acquisition of Los Altares, roughly 55,000 hectares in the Cerro Solo uranium district. The price was C$300,000 in cash, C$700,000 in shares and a 2% royalty. That works out to about C$18 per hectare up front, including the shares, on ground with roughly 12,500 metres of reported historical drilling.

That’s why I like Myriad’s chances if the sector rebound holds. Argentina took a modest bite out of the treasury, while the drilling in Wyoming could give investors something worth repricing the stock for: a first modern estimate of how many pounds Copper Mountain holds.

Disclosure: Paid partnership with Myriad Uranium. Please do your own research.

#Uranium $MYRUF $M.CN

Of the 100 companies in my uranium cash table below, Myriad is one I’d watch for a rebound. It reported C$11.54M in cash and equivalents at July 31. Management says it can fund drilling beyond the first 5,000 metres of Phase II at Copper Mountain in Wyoming.

What I like is where those metres are going. Union Pacific drilled roughly 2,000 holes in this district decades ago. Myriad now owns Copper Mountain outright and can use that work to choose where a new hole will tell it the most. The aim is to verify historical results and fill the gaps needed for a first NI 43-101 mineral resource estimate.

The October 28 update gives a sense of what they’re finding. At Hesitation, one hole returned 34.3 metres at 399 ppm eU₃O₈ in preliminary downhole gamma readings. I’m watching the lab assays next.

Then there’s what Myriad picked up in Argentina. On November 2, it announced the acquisition of Los Altares, roughly 55,000 hectares in the Cerro Solo uranium district. The price was C$300,000 in cash, C$700,000 in shares and a 2% royalty. That works out to about C$18 per hectare up front, including the shares, on ground with roughly 12,500 metres of reported historical drilling.

That’s why I like Myriad’s chances if the sector rebound holds. Argentina took a modest bite out of the treasury, while the drilling in Wyoming could give investors something worth repricing the stock for: a first modern estimate of how many pounds Copper Mountain holds.

Disclosure: Paid partnership with Myriad Uranium. Please do your own research.

The demand is already there. GeneDx reported 25% year-over-year growth in exome and genome testing volumes in Q3, with full-year growth guidance of at least 28%. More doctors are ordering genomic tests, more patients are being diagnosed, and the clinical value of this technology is becoming increasingly clear.

But here is the problem.

It is about changing the economics of tests GeneDx is already performing, while potentially opening the door to many more patients.

GeneDx has built a database from hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of genetic and clinical data points.

Sequencing DNA is becoming cheap. Understanding which mutations actually cause disease is much harder.

Without enough patient data, you cannot connect the dots.

You can buy sequencing machines, hire scientists, and build laboratories. What you cannot easily buy is years of accumulated clinical knowledge.

Every additional patient potentially strengthens that database, making it even harder for competitors to replicate.

This is the real moat of $WGS.

Anthony, the "spy" story appears to be as fake as Russiagate. Here are the facts as I understand them.

(1) First, Alice Huang was at a company called Megaspeed[1], which everyone agrees bought Nvidia chips to sell to Southeast Asian companies called neoclouds. This is in itself completely legal under US law.

(2) However, some both inside and outside the admin didn't like this. They want to block Chinese nationals from accessing cloud services with Nvidia GPUs even if those servers are located outside China. Fine, but the so-called Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to block this has passed the House but not the Senate, and is not law[2].

(3) Singapore's government also looked into this when Alice Huang was on their soil[3] and didn't find any evidence that Megaspeed was actually selling chips to China illegally — let alone that she was a "Chinese spy." They did give her an entry ban, but that's like a visa denial.

(4) The related point is that it's not actually illegal to sell Nvidia chips to China! Since the Biden admin, there has been a complex and constantly-shifting set of export restrictions on chips. As of right now, Nvidia is allowed to sell H200s[4] to China, and indeed has designed these to comply with applicable law.

(5) But you know what...China actually also doesn't want Nvidia chips in China [5,6], because they want to build up their homegrown chip industry. The Nvidia chips are so good that China doesn't want to remain dependent on American chips, or vulnerable to possible US backdoors.

(6) The broader point is that this is an argument between nationalists and capitalists. Nationalists argue that US companies shouldn't even get close to selling to China, and shouldn't even be selling to neoclouds, even if it's "technically" legal. Capitalists argue that it's impossible for American companies to dominate world markets without, you know, being allowed to dominate world markets by actually competing in them. And that it's one thing to restrict physical sales to China, and quite another to require proof-of-citizenship for every single cloud access.

(7) Here's the thing: it doesn't make sense for one of the (few!) industries where America has a trade surplus with China to be summarily cut off, if you're worried about trade surpluses. It doesn't make sense to remove your number one AI CEO, if you want to be number one in AI. And it truly doesn't make sense to do to Jensen Huang what the communists did to Jack Ma[7], if your goal is fighting communism.

(8) So, to summarize: there's no proof of spying, as Blanche at DOJ has admitted[8], which rebuts your FBI/DOJ points. The Wachtell investigation you raise is just an in-house thing[9] ordered by the Nvidia board. And so all that's left is some affairs, which society has agreed is not disqualifying, given the realities of both Clinton and Trump.

In short: do you want a communist society like China, where Jack Ma's company can be stolen from him overnight on false pretenses? Or do you want some semblance of rule of law? If so, you should support the restoration of Jensen Huang to the company he built.

Frontier models can now propose technical social science research designs that experts grade more highly than the world's top political economist's---that's the finding from our new Free Systems eval, SnyderBench, in which we have PhD experts blind grade research proposals from AI models compared to papers written by Harvard political economist Jim Snyder (which the experts have not previously read). 

At the same time, we see no evidence that models can develop research ideas that experts rate as better overall contributions. They're getting better and better at the technical part of research, but not necessarily at the more subjective part.

This could be because human experts possess "judgment" that the models do not. 

It could also be that research "contribution" is so subjective that it doesn't actually point at any meaningful goal---consistent with this possibility, we find that our human experts don't agree with one another when rating project ideas for the strength of their contribution, with agreement rates barely higher than random chance. Perhaps social science research is what @alexolegimas might call a "relational good": something people value in part because it's produced by a human. We're not sure. 

This past January, I released the results of a pilot in which I had Claude Code replicate and extend a past empirical paper on vote-by-mail. 10 months later, it's stunning the amount of progress that's been made. It's no longer interesting to ask whether AI can collect data and run analyses automagically---we take that for granted---instead, the question is how much of the entire research loop AI can complete. Our tentative answer: AI can handle the technical aspects of empirical political economy research from end to end, devising the design and executing it, but for now, we still need humans to drive the agenda. 

This is joint work with @AndyCWMyers, and is of course dedicated to my PhD advisor Jim Snyder, who remains the world's great empirical political economist, AI or no AI. 

Lots more in the full piece here:

https://freesystems.substack.com/p/benchmarking-ais-research-taste-in
